round1.text:
Every night, a fox climbed a hill to sit beneath the moon.

He told her small things: where the blackberries grew, what he had mistaken for a bird, which paths he disliked walking alone.

The moon began waiting for him.

Neither returned to the pond.

Then, one evening, the fox climbed the hill with a small, unimportant story he had saved for her.

Halfway through, he looked toward the pond.

sheet.title: Tom's First Takes
sheet.heading: Tom, the opening and the ending
sheet.lede: Tom read the first and last groups of the fable twice each. Choose one take for each group. The lines borrowed from the neighbouring groups are already cut away, so this is the reading the film would use.
notes: Once through, on the phone's own speaker, not headphones.
The opening: someone telling it rather than performing it. The list read as a list, and "The moon began waiting for him." landing without being pushed.
The ending: "The moon looked too." should stay open, not settle like the last line of a story. Each ending take runs on into the 3 seconds of silence before the title.

g2.text:
From so far away, each found the other easy to love.

One evening, she asked him to meet her beside a pond.

There, she could lay her reflection close enough for him to rest his head beside it.

For many nights, they were happy.

She lit the paths he had been afraid to walk. He told her stories about the world beneath the trees, where she had never been.

But there were things the fox did not like anyone to see.

cut.head: He told her stories about the world beneath the trees, where she had never been.

g3.text:
He told her stories about the world beneath the trees, where she had never been.

But there were things the fox did not like anyone to see.

When he was frightened, he hid. When he was ashamed, he pretended he had somewhere else to go.

The moon had her own difficulty. When someone grew quiet, she felt herself disappearing.

So when the fox withdrew beneath the reeds, she shone a little brighter.

She wanted him to know she was still there.

But now he could see the whole of himself in the water: his muddy coat, his trembling legs, the face he made when he was trying not to cry.

He asked for a little darkness.

She dimmed her light.

cut.head: He asked for a little darkness.
cut.tail: She rose away from the pond.

g4.text:
He asked for a little darkness.

She dimmed her light. For a while, they rested together.

But when he stayed quiet, she began to wonder whether he wanted her there at all.

Her light crept back across the pond.

The fox pulled a branch over the water.

He meant to make a hiding place.

From beneath the leaves, the moon watched her face disappear.

She rose away from the pond.

cut.head: From beneath the leaves, the moon watched her face disappear.
cut.tail: Then, one evening, the fox climbed the hill with a small, unimportant story he had saved for her.

g5.text:
From beneath the leaves, the moon watched her face disappear.

She rose away from the pond.

The fox pushed the branch aside and reached after her. His paw struck the water, breaking her reflection into pieces.

By the time the pond was still, she was high above the hill again.

For several nights, he slept without being seen.

For several nights, she crossed the sky without wondering whether she was welcome.

Neither was hurt again.

Neither returned to the pond.

Then, one evening, the fox climbed the hill with a small, unimportant story he had saved for her.

sheet.title: Tom's Middle Takes
sheet.heading: Tom, the middle of the fable
sheet.lede: Tom read the four middle groups (¶5–28) twice each, to go between the opening and the ending you chose. Choose one take for each group. The lines borrowed from the neighbouring groups are already cut away, so this is the reading the film would use.
notes: Once through, on the phone's own speaker, not headphones.
Someone telling it rather than performing it: uneven tempo, plain words stressed, nothing pushed.
Group 3: the stress on frightened, ashamed, disappearing and cry; what he sees in the water read as a list; and "He asked for a little darkness." said simply, because a silence follows it.
Group 4: the branch told plainly, with no blame in it, and "…watched her face disappear." left to land.
Group 5: his reach told as regret, not drama, and the two "Neither…" lines kept level.
